```{r}
library(z3r)
ctx <- z3_context()
```

## Bit-vectors

Bit-vectors are fixed-width machine integers: arithmetic wraps around modulo
2^width, and the same bits can be read as signed or unsigned. z3r never mixes
bit-vectors with unbounded integers, and operations whose meaning depends on
the sign come in two versions.

```{r}
x <- z3_bv(ctx, "x", 8)
z3_simplify(z3_bv_val(ctx, 255, 8) + 1)
z3_value(z3_bv_val(ctx, 200, 8))
z3_value(z3_bv_val(ctx, 200, 8), signed = TRUE)
```

`<` is deliberately not defined; use `z3_bvult()` (unsigned) or `z3_bvslt()`
(signed):

```{r, error = TRUE}
x < 3
```

### Verifying a bit trick for every input

A classic branch-free absolute value for 32-bit integers is
`(x ^ m) - m` with `m = x >> 31` (arithmetic shift). Is it equal to the
obvious definition for **all** 2^32 inputs? Ask Z3 for a counterexample:

```{r}
v <- z3_bv(ctx, "v", 32)
m <- z3_bvashr(v, 31)
trick <- z3_bvxor(v, m) - m
obvious <- z3_ite(z3_bvslt(v, 0), -v, v)
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, trick != obvious)
z3_check(s)
```

`"unsat"`: no counterexample exists, a proof over all inputs. A plausible but
wrong variant fails, and Z3 produces the counterexample:

```{r}
wrong <- z3_bvxor(v, m) + m
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, wrong != obvious)
z3_check(s)
z3_value(z3_eval(z3_model(s), v), signed = TRUE)
```

## Arrays

Z3 arrays are total maps from one sort to another:

```{r}
I <- z3_int_sort(ctx)
a <- z3_array(ctx, "a", I, I)
i <- z3_int(ctx, "i")
j <- z3_int(ctx, "j")
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
# Writing a[i] never changes a[j] for j != i
z3_add(s, i != j, z3_select(z3_store(a, i, 42), j) != z3_select(a, j))
z3_check(s)
```

## Strings

Strings are Unicode sequences with length, containment, substring and
conversion functions. Positions are 0-based.

```{r}
pw <- z3_string(ctx, "pw")
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s,
  z3_length(pw) == 8,
  z3_prefixof("R", pw),
  z3_contains(pw, "42"),
  z3_str_to_int(z3_substr(pw, 6, 2)) == 99
)
z3_check(s)
z3_value(z3_eval(z3_model(s), pw))
```

## Uninterpreted functions

An uninterpreted function is an unknown function with typed arguments. Z3
only knows that equal arguments give equal results, which is often all an
argument needs:

```{r}
f <- z3_function(ctx, "f", list(I), I)
x <- z3_int(ctx, "x")
y <- z3_int(ctx, "y")
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, x == y, f(x) != f(y))
z3_check(s)
```

Models give function tables:

```{r}
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, f(1) == 10, f(2) == 20)
z3_check(s)
z3_model(s)
```

## Quantifiers

`z3_forall()` and `z3_exists()` bind ordinary constants:

```{r}
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, z3_forall(x, f(x) >= x), f(3) < 3)
z3_check(s)
```

Quantifiers take Z3 outside decidable territory, so `"unknown"` answers are
possible. Patterns (`patterns = list(list(f(x)))`) guide instantiation.

## Tactics and goals

Tactics transform sets of formulas. They are useful for preprocessing and for
seeing what Z3 can derive:

```{r}
g <- z3_goal(ctx)
z3_add(g, x == y + 1, y > 2, x < 10)
t <- z3_tactic_then(z3_tactic(ctx, "simplify"), z3_tactic(ctx, "solve-eqs"))
z3_goal_formulas(z3_apply_tactic(t, g)[[1]])
head(z3_tactics(ctx))
```

## SMT-LIB2

SMT-LIB2 is the standard exchange format between solvers. z3r writes and
reads it with Z3's own printer and parser:

```{r}
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, x > 2, x < 5)
txt <- z3_to_smtlib(s)
cat(txt)
fs <- z3_from_smtlib(ctx, txt)
fs
```

Declared names map back to the same constants (`x` here is the same object
as `z3_int(ctx, "x")`). Raw SMT-LIB2 commands can also be run directly:

```{r}
cat(z3_eval_smtlib(ctx, "
  (declare-const k Int)
  (assert (= (* 3 k) 12))
  (check-sat)
  (get-value (k))
"))
```
